 Chiquita Canyon Landfill methane eruption prompts LA County probe, relocation aid
 By KJ Hiramoto  and  Alexa Mae Asperin Los Angeles County Updated  November 17, 2026 7:16 AM PST Published  November 16, 2026 5:01 PM PST Updated  November 17, 2026 7:16 AM PST ▾ LA Public Health, fire chief under fire over Chiquita Canyon explosion 
 LA County Supervisor Kathryn Barger is criticizing LA County Health and fire officials on their response to the geyser of methane and landfill debris at the Chiquita Canyon landfill.
 The Brief
 A routine drilling operation at Chiquita Canyon Landfill struck a pressurized methane pocket Monday, erupting hundreds of feet into the air. 
 Six workers were treated at the scene with four hospitalized as a precaution, while overnight air monitoring detected no immediate hazardous gas levels. 
 County supervisors unanimously passed an emergency motion demanding a full investigation and criticizing the Department of Public Health's delayed response. 
 LOS ANGELES COUNTY, Calif. - A routine drilling operation at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Castaic area struck a pressurized pocket of methane on Monday afternoon, sending a dark geyser of gas and decomposing garbage up to 500 feet into the air. 
 Following the eruption, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health ordered the landfill operator to provide voluntary relocation assistance to impacted residents, while the Board of Supervisors unanimously approved an emergency motion demanding a full investigation into the incident and the county's response.
 What we know:
 The Los Angeles County Fire Department responded to the facility in the 29200 block of Henry Mayo Drive at about 4:04 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 16, after the incident was initially reported as a commercial structure fire.
 Crews determined there was no fire, and instead found that an auger drilling a hole about 150 feet deep and three feet wide to install a new well—meant to address an ongoing elevated temperature landfill event—had struck a pocket of naturally occurring landfill gas. 
 Los Angeles County Fire Capt. Aaron Katon attributed the plume's initial dark-black color to decomposing trash, though the emissions later turned white and diminished dramatically before members of the fire department's Health and Hazardous Materials team capped the leak just after 10 p.m. and secured it by 11 p.m. Monday.
 Six nearby workers were treated at the scene, and four of them were transported to a hospital out of an abundance of caution with minor injuries or for evaluation, though the landfill's official statement reported no injuries.
 Engineers, hazardous materials teams, and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency representatives conducted overnight air quality monitoring at the site, around its perimeter, and in adjacent communities, finding zero readings for hazardous gases and reporting no health risk, officials said. 
 According to South Coast Air Quality Management District senior public affairs specialist Connie Villanueva, the facility's network of 12 monitoring stations takes hourly near-real-time measurements for hydrogen sulfide, methane, benzene, and other compounds. 
 While an evacuation advisory was briefly issued for zones CAS-VALVERDE-A, CAS-HASLEY, CAS-HILLCREST, CAS-CAMBRIDGE, and CAS-INDUSTRY, Fire Chief Anthony Marrone noted that first responders quickly determined formal evacuation orders were unnecessary and that the public was safe.
 What we don't know:
 While fire officials and landfill operators confirmed that a pressurized pocket of methane was struck during well installation, the exact failure of site safeguards remains under investigation. 
 County leaders have demanded full explanations regarding why the eruption occurred during a routine operation and what specific preventative measures failed to contain the pressurized pocket before it breached the surface. 
 Additionally, the exact medical conditions of the six evaluated workers have not been released.
 What they're saying:
 In an official statement, Chiquita Canyon Landfill stated that work was stopped immediately, and the area was secured without any release of liquids. 
 "As a precaution, Chiquita is reviewing data from all local air quality monitoring equipment," the operator stated. "The safety of our employees and the surrounding community is our highest priority. We will provide updates as more information becomes available."
 Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger, whose Fifth District includes Castaic, called the explosion and methane plume "unacceptable" and demanded strict accountability from the operator. 
 "The families of Castaic and the surrounding communities have lived with the burden of this landfill for far too long, and they should not have to wonder whether they are safe," Barger said in a statement. "I want answers, and I will not accept vague explanations. What happened at the site today, why it happened, and what safeguards failed are questions the operator and every responsible agency must answer fully and promptly. Those responsible will be held accountable."
 During Tuesday's Board of Supervisors meeting, Barger also criticized the Department of Public Health for failing to respond to the scene until her office demanded it around 8 p.m., which she said created a nearly four-hour information vacuum that fueled misinformation about evacuation orders and airborne materials. 
 "Last night, I was embarrassed," Barger told Public Health Director Barbara Ferrer during the meeting. 
 "I was embarrassed for you and I was embarrassed for your team. ... I saw firsthand and talked to people that are terrified, and are terrified now, questioning whether information that has been provided in the past is accurate," Ferrer said.
 Ferrer apologized for the delay, explaining that there was "a fair amount of confusion" and that her department was not immediately "looped in" to interagency discussions about potential public threats, though she believed a strike team member was dispatched around 6 p.m. and conceded her agency should have been involved earlier.
 Barger also issued the following statement later in the day:
 "Families in Val Verde should never have had to wonder whether it was safe to stay in their own homes.  
 Chiquita Canyon Landfill’s announcement that it will pay for three nights of hotel rooms for some residents is a step in the right direction, but it is not nearly enough. Three nights does not undo a four-year ordeal, and it does not answer the questions residents are asking about what they were exposed to yesterday. 
 I will be watching closely to make sure every eligible family gets the help they need. 
 This afternoon, my colleagues on the Board joined me in approving my motion for a full public accounting of yesterday’s incident. County departments will report back to the Board on November 24. Residents deserve transparency and real relief, not temporary fixes, and I will keep pushing until they get both." 
 What's next:
 On Tuesday, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved an emergency motion introduced by Barger requiring county departments to deliver a comprehensive report on both the landfill eruption and the multi-agency emergency response next week. 
 The motion also directs the Department of Mental Health to deploy resources in the Val Verde and Castaic areas, including support groups, stress management, and individual and family counseling. 
 What you can do:
 Although fire officials reported no hazardous air readings, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health warned that strong odors from the incident can cause headaches, nausea, dizziness, and irritation of the eyes, nose, and throat. 
 Health officials urge residents to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and run air conditioning on recirculation whenever odors become strong.
 Under the new county directive, affected residents are eligible for voluntary relocation assistance provided by Chiquita Canyon Landfill, which includes access to cooling centers, short-term hotel stays, transportation assistance, and air purifiers for those remaining at home. 
 Residents can review the full public health directive on the Los Angeles County website and are advised to rely on official county sources for ongoing updates.
 The Source: This report is based on official statements and updates from the Los Angeles County Fire Department, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, Chiquita Canyon Landfill, and the South Coast Air Quality Management District. Additional details and direct quotes were gathered from City News Service reporting, public statements by Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger, and proceedings from Tuesday's Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors meeting.
